item.title: Tumor Treating Fields and Quality of Life Among Patients With Locally Advanced Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: The PANOVA-3 trial demonstrated the survival benefit and tolerability of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, but understanding the impact of TTFields therapy on quality of life (QoL) and pain is important for clinical decision-making.

Objective: To analyze the impact of TTFields therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel on QoL and pain outcomes using prospective data from PANOVA-3.

Design, setting, and participants: This is a prespecified secondary analysis of PANOVA-3, which was a global, open-label, multicenter, phase 3 randomized clinical trial in adult patients with previously untreated locally advanced unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma (LA-PAC). A total of 571 patients were randomized between May 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023, with follow-up completed October 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from November 2024 to May 2025.

Intervention: Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTFields therapy (150 kHz) with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. Nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m2) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2) were administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of 28-day cycles. Duration of follow-up was 18 months.

Main outcomes and measures: QoL was measured using the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire and the 26-item pancreatic cancer module. End points were mean changes from baseline QoL scores, deterioration-free survival of QoL, and time to opioid use. An analysis of pain medication use was performed post hoc.

Results: At baseline, 562 patients (median [IQR] age, 67 [31-90] years; 295 [52.5%] female), including 279 of 285 patients in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm and 283 of 286 patients in the gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm, completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire. Global health status was stable during the 26-month follow-up in both study arms. Digestive symptoms, pain, and pancreatic pain were improved from 2 months after treatment initiation throughout treatment and follow-up in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm. TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel was associated with longer deterioration-free survival for global health status than gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone (median [IQR], 7.1 [3.5-14.8] vs 5.7 [2.3-11.5] months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 95% CI, 0.61-0.97; P = .02). Longer deterioration-free survival was also observed for most items on the digestive symptoms scales (indigestion and altered bowel habit were similar between the 2 arms). Median (IQR) deterioration-free survival was significantly longer with TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel for pain (10.1 [4.0-20.9] vs 7.4 [3.5-14.5] months; HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.89; P = .003) and pancreatic pain (14.7 [6.2-46.2] vs 10.2 [5.6-18.2] months; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.52-0.90; P = .006) as was median time to opioid use in the modified intention-to-treat population (9.3 [3.9-18.6] vs 6.7 [1.1-16.3] months; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; P = .01).

Conclusions and relevance: This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that TTFields therapy with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel improved QoL and provided clinically meaningful benefits in pain outcomes compared with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. This study's results suggest that TTFields therapy with gemicitabine and nab-paclitaxel is practice-changing for patients with unresectable LA-PAC.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03377491.

item.title: Clinician Training, Text Messages, and Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Among Children Aged 10 to 12 Years: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rates among adolescents remain below recommendations.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician communication training and parent-targeted text messages at increasing HPV vaccination among children aged 11 to 12 years.

Design, setting, and participants: This doubly randomized, 2-level nested clinical trial was conducted from February 2022 to September 2024 among clinicians at 30 pediatric primary care clinics in Florida, children aged 10 to 12 years who had not received any of the 3 adolescent HPV vaccines, and their parents. Interventions occurred for 1 year, and vaccine records were collected for 2 years.

Interventions: Clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 training groups: (1) the bundled approach, which presents the HPV vaccine in the middle of 2 other recommended vaccines; (2) the focused approach, which emphasizes cancer prevention; and (3) deferred, which offered clinicians the opportunity to participate in the focused training after the trial concluded. Clinicians in the first 2 groups completed a 1-hour communication training and a 5-minute booster session. Patients within clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 text message groups, aligned with the communication strategies: (1) bundled, (2) focused, and (3) no text messages. Parents were sent text messages at the start of the study or prior to their child's 11th birthday as well as prior to appointments.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were HPV vaccine initiation (receipt of first dose) and completion (receipt of second dose). Analyses accounted for clinic-level clustering. Effects were analyzed as randomized and text messages as received.

Results: At baseline, 59 clinicians (44 [75%] female; 12 [20%] Asian, 21 [36%] Hispanic, and 21 [36%] non-Hispanic White) within 30 randomized clinics were included, with 17 randomized to the focused group, 21 to the bundled group, and 21 to the deferred group. A total of 7234 children were aged 10 (3576 [49%]), 11 (2617 [36%]), and 12 (1041 [14%]) years at study start (1673 [23%] Hispanic, 1001 [14%] non-Hispanic Black, and 1210 [17%] non-Hispanic White). A total of 28 clinics (93%), 50 clinicians (85%), and 6498 children (90%) completed the 2-year follow-up. The mean pre-post clinic-level difference for HPV vaccine initiation was 28.2 (95% CI, 25.3-31.1) percentage points and for completion was 16.1 (95% CI, 13.3-18.9) percentage points. Risk ratios for clinician training and text messaging did not differ between groups for initiation or completion. Among patients whose parents received text messages vs not, the risk ratio for initiation was 1.17 (95% CI, 1.08-1.26) and for completion was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.06-1.56).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study of Florida children aged 10 to 12 years, clinic-level HPV vaccination increased over time. No differences in HPV vaccination by random assignment of clinician training or text messages were detected. When received, text messages were associated with higher HPV vaccination.

item.title: Body Mass Index Peak-Rebound Patterns and Inhibitory Control Among Young Children
item.description:
Importance: Childhood obesity has been linked with poor inhibitory control, and atypical body mass index (BMI) growth trajectories may identify children at higher risk for poor inhibitory control. Inhibitory control is also sexually dimorphic (male vs female), as maladaptive inhibitory control is more common in males.

Objective: To investigate the association between early childhood BMI peak-rebound patterns and inhibitory control development at 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years and test whether there is a sexually dimorphic association.

Design, setting, and participants: The Programming Research in Obesity, Growth, Environment, and Social Stressors study is a prebirth cohort that recruited pregnant women receiving prenatal care through the Mexican Social Security Institute from July 2007 to February 2010 and followed up from pregnancy through age 8 years. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to December 2025.

Exposure: Repeated weight and length or height measurements were collected from birth to 8 years and mixed-effects models were used to characterize sex- and child-specific BMI trajectories and derive age and magnitude of the BMI peak (maximum inflection point during infancy) and rebound (minimum inflection point during early childhood).

Main outcomes and measures: Children completed the Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance Test, second edition, to assess inhibitory control at ages 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years, and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess associations of age and magnitude of BMI peak and rebound with inhibitory control across the 2 time points. Sex-specific trajectories were evaluated by modeling interactions between child sex.

Results: Among 539 children included in the study, 278 (51.6%) were male; 277 (51.4%) were born to mothers with low socioeconomic status, and the mean (SD) gestational age at birth was 38.4 (1.6) weeks. After adjusting for covariates, a 1-SD higher BMI at peak was associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time standard errors (β = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.20 to 1.58). A 1-SD higher age at rebound was associated with higher hit reaction time (β = 2.35; 95% CI, -0.01 to 4.72). However, age at peak and BMI at rebound were not associated with any inhibitory control measure. Children with early timing of peak and rebound exhibited higher T-scores for omission errors (β = 4.05; 95% CI, 0.96 to 7.13), while children with early timing of peak and late timing of BMI rebound had lower T-scores for hit reaction time (β = -4.16; 95% CI, -7.29 to -1.02) compared with those with normal timing of peak and rebound. In males, both older age and a higher magnitude of BMI rebound were associated with lower omission error T-scores, whereas in females, variations in age and magnitude of BMI patterns were associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time and hit reaction time standard errors.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 539 children in Mexico, early-life BMI peak-rebound trajectories across childhood were associated with inhibitory control. These findings extend the literature beyond the well-established effects of BMI peak-rebound on metabolic conditions.

item.title: Access to Care and Practice Variation in the Assessment of Ankyloglossia
item.description:
Importance: Diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia has increased in recent years. A lack of universal evaluation and management guidelines may contribute to inconsistent practice patterns and variable access to care.

Objective: To evaluate access to care and practice pattern variation in the treatment of ankyloglossia as a source of breastfeeding difficulty across clinicians and sites of care in Ohio.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study of pediatric dentists and pediatric and general otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients in Ohio was conducted using a secret shopper approach from October 6, 2025, to January 5, 2026. All pediatric dentists and otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients were eligible for inclusion. Health care professionals were identified using lists obtained from the Ohio State Dental Board and the American Academy of Otolaryngology.

Exposure: Clinics were contacted via phone by a simulated patient's mother using a vignette describing a 2-week-old infant with breastfeeding difficulty characterized by painful latch and inquiring regarding ankyloglossia (ie, tongue tie) evaluation.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were time to first available appointment and procedure cost to patient on the day of service. Secondary outcomes included referral requirement, potential for same-day procedures, procedure technique, additional procedures discussed during scheduling, insurance acceptance, and total cost of consultation and procedure.

Results: A total of 175 clinics representing 487 health care professionals (299 dentists and 188 otolaryngologists) were contacted. The median (IQR) appointment wait time was 14 (7-28) days. For practices providing cost information, time-of-service cash payment was required by 31 of 36 dental offices (86%), while all otolaryngology practices (38 of 38; [100%]) billed medical insurance. Dental clinics were more likely to empirically recommend other procedures (eg, maxillary frenulum release) at the time of appointment scheduling (29 of 45 [64%]) than otolaryngology offices (1 of 38 [3%]) (P < .001). Across all practices, the median (IQR) cost of lingual frenotomy alone was $474 ($350-$545), while total cost (consultation and all recommended procedures) ranged from $200 to $1515.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of pediatric dental and otolaryngology clinics in Ohio, access to care for ankyloglossia was similar, but the anticipated cost of procedures varied widely, as did empiric recommendations for intervention beyond lingual frenotomy. Prospective patients should be aware of this heterogeneity and the potential for significant price differences for treatment.

item.title: Work Hours, Emergency Department Context, and Workplace Violence Among Nurses
item.description:
Importance: Workplace violence is common in high-risk health care settings, with consequences for clinician well-being and care delivery. Less is known about multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence in emergency department (ED) nurses.

Objective: To characterize workplace violence among ED nurses and identify multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used nurse survey data combined with administrative and electronic medical record data collected in 2023 from nurses working in 11 EDs in a multisite health system in the southeastern US.

Exposure: Multilevel work-system factors, with primary exposures of interest including overtime, shift type, and ED type (freestanding vs in-hospital); additional covariates included individual, team, and ED-level characteristics.

Main outcomes and measures: Any self-reported workplace violence in the prior month (threats, physical violence, verbal abuse, unwanted sexual attention, or bullying) from patients, visitors, and/or coworkers. Associations were estimated using mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for emergency department site and factor selection using cross-validated least absolute shrinkage and selectrion operator regression. Nurses in the supplemental staffing team were excluded from this analysis.

Results: Among 337 ED nurses (mean [SD] age, 34.9 [9.5] years; 289 [85.8%] female; 287 [85.2% white; mean [SD] nursing experience, 9.0 [8.2] years), 296 (87.8%) reported workplace violence in the prior month. Incidents of WPV involved patients or visitors (292 of 296 [98.6%]) and coworkers (60 of 296 [20.3%]). In adjusted mixed-effects models (n = 299), overtime was associated with higher odds of workplace violence (OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.30-7.93), while night shift (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.78) and employment in a freestanding ED (OR, 0.25; 95% CI, 0.09-0.76) were associated with lower odds.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of ED nurses, workplace violence was common and was associated with overtime and ED context. These findings support further evaluation of work-hour practices and context-specific approaches to workplace violence prevention.

item.title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in County-Level Availability of Uterine Cancer Clinical Trials
item.description:
Importance: Racial and ethnic disparities exist in clinical trial enrollment, but whether such disparities exist in geographic availability of uterine cancer trials is unknown.

Objective: To examine associations between race and ethnicity and county-level presence and rates of available uterine cancer clinical trials.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study linked Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Research Plus; Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov; and American Community Survey data of adult patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with uterine cancer between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2021. The data analysis was performed between November 10, 2025, and September 9, 2026.

Exposures: Race and ethnicity categorized as American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic (any race), Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were county-level presence and rate of interventional uterine cancer trials. Hurdle models were used to estimate racial and ethnic differences in the odds of residing in a county with at least 1 trial and among patients in counties with trial availability, differences in rates of trials per person. Models accounted for county clustering and were adjusted for patient characteristics.

Results: Among 155 811 patients in the cohort (median [IQR] age at diagnosis, 62 [55-69] years; 1055 identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native [0.7%], 12 753 as Asian [8.2%], 16 303 as Black [10.5%], 23 177 as Hispanic [14.9%], 2175 as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander [1.4%], and 100 348 as White [64.4%] race and ethnicity), 121 525 (78.0%) resided in a county with at least 1 available trial. Trial availability was observed among 58.0% of American Indian or Alaska Native patients, 94.3% of Asian patients, 77.7% of Black patients, 86.1% of Hispanic patients, 90.3% of Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander patients, and 74.1% of White patients. Compared with White patients, higher odds of residing in counties with at least 1 available trial were found for Asian (odds ratio [OR], 5.83; 95% CI, 4.83-7.12), Black (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.07-1.30), Hispanic (OR, 2.18; 95% CI, 1.80-2.63), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (OR, 3.34; 95% CI, 2.17-5.66) patients, whereas American Indian or Alaska Native patients had lower odds (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.39-0.61). Among patients in counties with at least 1 trial, fewer available trials per person were found for Asian (rate ratio [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.74), Hispanic (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.52-0.61), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.80-0.95) patients compared with White patients.

Conclusions and relevance: This cohort study of patients with uterine cancer found that racial and ethnic patterns in geographic trial availability differed by how availability was measured. The presence of any trial may not fully capture geographic access to clinical trial opportunities.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposome at Birth and Trajectories of Epigenetic Age Acceleration Across Childhood
item.description:
Importance: Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) has been linked to increased disease risk in adults, yet its developmental trajectories and early-life neighborhood determinants remain poorly understood.

Objective: To examine whether there are associations between the neighborhood exposome at birth and EAA trajectories from early childhood through adolescence.

Design, setting, and participants: This longitudinal cohort study used data from Project Viva, a prebirth cohort that enrolled pregnant women in eastern Massachusetts from April 22, 1999, to July 31, 2002. Participants included 570 children with available peripheral blood DNA methylation data, complete neighborhood characteristics, and complete covariates. Data were analyzed from August 19, 2024, to August 21, 2026.

Exposures: Neighborhood exposome profiles at birth derived from 22 census tract-level characteristics across 4 domains (area deprivation, social fragmentation, population density, and environmental quality) using self-organizing maps.

Main outcomes and measures: EAA was calculated at 3, 8, and 13 years of age using the Horvath, Skin & Blood, and Wu epigenetic clocks. Trajectories were identified using latent class linear mixed models. Associations between neighborhood profiles and EAA trajectories were estimated using multinomial mixed models.

Results: Among 570 children (mean [SD] age at early childhood, 3.2 [0.4] years; 305 [53.5%] male), 3 EAA trajectory groups (stable, increasing, and decreasing for the Horvath and Skin & Blood clocks or low-baseline for the Wu clock) and 3 neighborhood profiles were identified. Compared with profile 1 (suburban, lowest adverse exposures [n = 278]), children born into profile 2 (urban, high residential instability and single-person households, and highway proximity [n = 168]) had greater odds of increasing EAA for the Wu clock (adjusted odds ratio, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.03-2.69]). Profile 3 (urban, high socioeconomic deprivation and pollution [n = 124]) showed no associations.

Conclusions and relevance: In this longitudinal cohort study, birth into neighborhoods characterized by high residential instability and single-person households and highway proximity was associated with increasing Wu EAA trajectories across childhood. These findings suggest that early-life neighborhood conditions, encompassing both social and physical environmental factors, may represent targets for interventions aimed at reducing long-term disease risk. Further research is needed to clarify the implications of these findings for later health and prevention.

item.title: Publicly Available Information on Insurance Coverage for Maternal-Fetal Surgery
item.description:
Importance: Maternal-fetal surgery has expanded rapidly in the US, but how insurance coverage supports delivery of this specialized, high-cost care has not been systematically characterized.

Objective: To characterize publicly ascertainable information about how Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers cover procedures used in maternal-fetal surgery.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional descriptive study analyzed insurance coverage policies in the US from March through August 2025. Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers were selected based on national market share.

Exposure: Insurance coverage policies for maternal-fetal surgery-related procedures were assessed using publicly available fee schedules and structured outreach to payer representatives.

Main outcomes and measures: Coverage status (covered, not covered, or data not available) for 19 maternal-fetal surgery-related Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) and Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) codes and 5 comparator codes.

Results: The study included 50 state Medicaid programs and 30 large commercial insurers. Among Medicaid programs, coverage was high for nonspecific or individual components of procedures (eg, intrauterine transfusion: 49 of 49 available determinations [100%]) but incomplete and highly variable for codes specific to comprehensive interventions (eg, 6 of 36 available determinations [16.7%] for in utero sacrococcygeal teratoma resection). Among 44 states with available determinations for both code types, mean (SD) coverage was higher for CPT codes than S-codes (86.3% [14.1%] vs 53.0% [37.0%]; P < .001), with consistent findings in sensitivity analyses. The median (range) proportion of MFS-related codes covered per state was 14.5 (0-19) of 19 codes (76.3%). Among 5 commercial insurers with data, all 5 (100.0%) reported coverage of all 4 S-codes representing comprehensive interventions.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, coverage of maternal-fetal surgery-related codes was incomplete and variable, and transparency in commercial coverage policies was limited. These findings suggest that coverage uncertainty may complicate health-system planning and financing for this increasingly used, high-cost care.

item.title: Procalcitonin- and Presepsin-Guided Antibiotics for Early-Onset Sepsis in Preterm Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Early administration of antibiotics in the absence of proven sepsis, such as for treatment of early-onset sepsis (EOS), has been associated with adverse outcomes in very preterm infants. Reference values for procalcitonin (PCT) and presepsin (P-SEP) have been established in preterm infants.

Objective: To determine whether PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment for EOS was noninferior to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity.

Design, setting, and participants: This randomized multicenter noninferiority clinical trial was conducted in 17 Italian neonatal intensive care units between June 1, 2023, and January 31, 2025, among preterm infants born at 25 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation.

Interventions: Enrolled infants were randomly allocated to receive either PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment, administered if PCT and P-SEP levels exceeded prespecified thresholds, or universal antibiotic treatment for EOS.

Main outcomes and measures: The composite primary outcome was defined as survival without late-onset sepsis (LOS), bronchopulmonary dysplasia, grade 3 or 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), grade 2 or higher necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or stage 3 or higher retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The prespecified noninferiority margin was -5 percentage points. Both a primary intention-to-treat analysis and a secondary per-protocol analysis were performed, as recommended for noninferiority trials.

Results: The study enrolled and randomized 283 very preterm infants (mean [SD] gestational age, 30.2 [2.2] weeks; 161 girls [57%]); 143 received procalcitonin- and presepsin-guided treatment and 140 received universal antibiotic treatment. The primary outcome did not differ between the PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment group and the universal antibiotic treatment groups (76 of 143 [53%] vs 77 of 140 [55%]; risk difference, -1.8 percentage points; 90% CI, -11.9 to 8.3 percentage points; P = .32). Noninferiority of PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment compared with universal treatment was not demonstrated, because the lower bound of the 2-sided 90% CI crossed the prespecified noninferiority margin. The risk differences for LOS, IVH, NEC, PVL, ROP, and death were not significantly different between the groups. PCT and P-SEP values were not different between the groups. No patient developed EOS.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial conducted among neonates born between 25 weeks and 0 days and 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation, a PCT- and P-SEP-guided strategy for the treatment of EOS did not demonstrate noninferiority to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Within the limits of this study, these findings do not support the routine use of a biomarker-guided approach as an alternative to universal treatment for this high-risk population.

item.title: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities in Preschoolers With Bilateral Cerebral Palsy: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Intensive interventions for children with cerebral palsy (CP) have traditionally focused on the upper extremities, despite frequent impairments in gross motor function and the critical period of motor development occurring before age 5 years. Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) has demonstrated efficacy in improving manual dexterity and gross motor function in school-aged children, but evidence in preschool children with bilateral CP remains limited.

Objective: To determine whether early HABIT-ILE improves gross motor function more than usual unstructured motor activities in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter randomized clinical trial was conducted between December 2019 and December 2021. Recruitment was from European university hospitals, CP-specialized centers, and spontaneous applications at 4 sites: Brussels, Belgium; Brest and Angers, France; and Pisa, Italy. Children aged 12 to 59 months with spastic or dyskinetic bilateral CP who were able to follow instructions were included. Exclusion criteria were uncontrolled seizures, scheduled botulinum toxin injections or orthopedic surgery during the 6 months before or during the study period, severe visual or cognitive impairments, and contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging. Data were analyzed in May 2024.

Interventions: Children were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 2 weeks of usual motor activity, including usual rehabilitation (control group), or 2 weeks (50 hours) of HABIT-ILE (HABIT-ILE group).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66; range, 0-100, with lower scores indicating lesser gross motor ability). Secondary outcomes included Both Hand Assessment (BoHA), Melbourne Assessment 2, Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory-Computer Adaptive Test (PEDI-CAT), and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). Assessments were performed at baseline (immediately before intervention) and 2 weeks and 3 months after baseline.

Results: Among 49 preschool children with CP (mean [SD] age, 40.18 [11.53] months; 18 girls [36.7%] and 31 boys [63.3%]), Gross Motor Function Classification levels were I in 5 children, II in 14 children, III in 17 children, and IV or V in 13 children and Mini-Manual Ability Classification levels were I in 10 children, II in 27 children, III in 7 children, and IV or V in 6 children. Change in mean (SD) GMFM-66 score from baseline to 3 months was significantly greater in the HABIT-ILE group (5.01 [2.52] logits) than the control group (0.70 [1.98] logits) (adjusted mean difference [aMD] in score, 4.33 logits; 95% CI, 3.03-5.62 logits; P < .001). Likewise, mean (SD) scores favored the HABIT-ILE group vs the control group for secondary outcomes of BoHA (5.32 [4.47] vs 0.13 [5.16]; aMD, 5.15; 95% CI, 2.23-8.08; P < .001), PEDI-CAT mobility domain (1.70 [2.18] vs -0.40 [4.38]; aMD, 2.27; 95% CI, 0.20-4.33; P = .03), and COPM performance (4.22 [1.61] vs 1.14 [1.35]; aMD, 3.55; 95% CI, 2.86-4.24; P < .001) and satisfaction (4.37 [1.38] vs 1.15 [1.63]; aMD, 3.11; 95% CI, 2.25-3.97; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, early HABIT-ILE significantly improved upper and lower extremities motor performance in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP at 3 months after the intervention. These findings suggest that HABIT-ILE is effective in improving gross motor function in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP.

item.title: Cumulative Stress and Health Care Utilization Among US Service Members
item.description:
Importance: Military personnel experience unique occupational stressors, which, combined with other life stressors, may substantially impact their health readiness. Stress exposure is known to be associated with health and health care concerns in civilian populations, but little is known as to whether these associations are present among US service members.

Objective: To evaluate the association between individual stressors, cumulative stress exposure, and health care utilization (HCU) among a contemporary sample of US service members.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort analysis used self-reported survey data from the Millennium Cohort Study and up to 3 years of inpatient and outpatient HCU data from Military Health System electronic health records (2020-2023) from US active-duty service members who first completed a Millennium Cohort Study baseline survey in 2020 and 2021. Data were analyzed from January to May 2026.

Exposure: Self-reported stress exposure (adverse childhood experiences, stressful life events, discrimination, bullying, hazing, and combat experiences) was assessed in 2020 and 2021.

Main outcomes and measures: Inpatient, outpatient, and total HCU patient-days were calculated. Negative binomial regression models examined the HCU association with cumulative and individual stress exposures, adjusting for demographic and military characteristics.

Results: A total of 34 731 service members were included in the analytic sample (33 252 [95.8%] were young adults aged 17-34 years; 9906 [28.5%] were female). They spent a mean (SD) of 17.74 (19.10) days (median [IQR], 12 [2-23] days) in outpatient and 0.61 (4.98) days (median [IQR], 0 [0-0] days) in inpatient care across a mean (SD) follow-up period of 2.08 (0.84) years. Higher cumulative stress exposure was associated with greater total (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.54; 95% CI, 1.50-1.57), inpatient (IRR, 2.28; 95% CI, 2.21-2.35), and outpatient (IRR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.47-1.54) HCU. Individual stressors, particularly adverse childhood experiences and stressful life events, were also associated with greater HCU.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of contemporary US active-duty service members, increased stress exposure was positively associated with greater HCU. Identifying and triaging various stress exposures during outpatient visits can support better access to inpatient care for service members. In turn, these efforts may translate into better patient outcomes, medical readiness, and military health system improvements.

item.title: Eating Disorders in Individuals With Celiac Disease and Their Biological First-Degree Relatives
item.description:
Importance: Patients with celiac disease (CD) may face elevated risk of eating disorders, potentially due to genetic susceptibility and psychosocial factors of a gluten-free diet. However, up-to-date population-based evidence is scarce, and whether any excess risk extends to biological first-degree relatives (bFDRs) remains unclear.

Objective: To investigate the risk of eating disorders in patients with CD and their bFDRs, including parents, full siblings, and offspring.

Design, setting, and participants: A nationwide multigenerational cohort study of patients with celiac disease in Sweden, observed from January 2002 to December 2023. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to August 2026. From Sweden's 28 histopathology departments, patients with biopsy-confirmed CD diagnosed 2002 to 2023 were identified. Each patient was matched with fewer than or equal to 5 general population reference individuals; bFDRs of patients with CD and reference individuals were also identified.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was any eating disorder. The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for eating disorders diagnosed at age 6 years or older were estimated using Cox regression and flexible parametric survival models for the overall and time-varying estimates, respectively.

Results: This study included 37 853 patients with CD (23 704 [62.6%] female; median [IQR] age at index date 28.7 [11.7-53.0] years ) and 185 159 reference individuals. Over 10.9 years median follow-up (IQR, 5.9-15.8 years), 485 patients with CD and 1578 reference individuals were diagnosed with any eating disorder. CD was associated with an increased hazard for eating disorders (aHR, 1.39; 95% CI,1.27-1.53), most apparent during the first 5 years of follow-up. Over 20 years of follow-up, 1 extra eating disorder case was expected per 222 patients with CD. In contrast, there was no hazard elevation for any eating disorder among CD-bFDRs (53 435 parents: aHR, 0.82 [0.61-1.12]; 48 743 siblings: aHR, 1.11 [0.99-1.24]; 38 695 offspring: aHR, 1.05 [0.92-1.20]). Sensitivity analyses mitigating information bias and residual confounding largely aligned with main findings.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients with CD, a moderately increased eating disorders risk particularly during the first 5 years of follow-up was observed, although the absolute risk was low. This increased risk did not extend to bFDRs of patients with CD. Clinical vigilance toward disordered eating is important among patients with newly diagnosed CD.

item.title: Family Presence Policies in Pediatric Intensive Care Units
item.description:
Importance: Family presence supports critically ill children, yet pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) policies remain inconsistent, creating inequities in access to parents or caregivers. Clear guidance is needed to support equitable, child-centered policy development.

Objective: To generate evidence-informed and knowledge user-informed recommendations for family presence policies in PICUs.

Design, setting, and participants: This survey study, conducted through surveys and virtual meetings, used a modified Delphi consensus process. Candidate items were derived from family presence guidance documents and PICU family presence research (environmental scan; scoping review; surveys and interviews with patients, families, and health care professionals; and focus groups). Items were organized into themes covering policy priorities; policy-making responsibilities; baseline and emergency policies; and policy communication, enforcement, and revision. From February 2024 to February 2025, panelists completed 2 rating rounds and 1 virtual meeting, with follow-up meetings and member-checking to incorporate input across knowledge user groups. Knowledge users included former PICU patients, family members, clinicians, and policymakers (hospital and PICU administrators and infection prevention and control specialists) from across Canada.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was consensus-derived policy priorities and recommendations for PICU family presence during baseline operations and emergency situations.

Results: Forty-three knowledge users, including 5 patients, 12 family members, 21 clinicians, and 5 policymakers (35 self-reported women or girls [81.4%]), agreed on 10 policy priorities and 44 recommendations. Key messages included that children should be at the center of policy-related decision-making and always have access to at least 2 primary caregivers; families should determine sibling presence and assume responsibility for it; policies should recognize the importance of visitors beyond family for the child's well-being; and policies should be flexible, adapting to different situations while adhering to core priorities. Recommendations addressed who should make policies; communication, enforcement, and change processes; number, type (eg, parents or caregivers, siblings, and visitors), and timing of bedside presence; family movement and supports; and approaches to personal protective equipment and infectious symptoms to preserve family presence, including during emergencies.

Conclusions and relevance: This survey study with consensus-based recommendations for PICU family presence provided a framework for policy design in routine and emergency contexts. The recommendations emphasized the patient's best interest and continued access to at least 2 primary caregivers. They supported context-specific and unit-specific policy design and may be broadly applicable across children's hospitals.

item.title: Civil Society Organization-Led Home Visit Intervention to Reduce Unintentional Child Injury in Rural China: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of childhood death and disability, but evidence on scalable home visit interventions in rural settings is limited.

Objective: To evaluate whether a civil society organization-led home visit intervention can reduce unintentional injuries among children and improve caregiver and household safety.

Design, setting, and participants: This outcome assessor-blinded cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 24 rural communities in Guizhou and Shaanxi, China, from May 6 to October 1, 2025. After baseline assessment, communities were randomized as clusters in a 1:1 ratio. Participants were households with children aged 3 to 12 years.

Interventions: Control communities received routine social worker home visits; intervention communities received routine services plus 3 monthly structured visits with home safety and first aid tool kits and a follow-up visit at month 4.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was caregiver-reported cumulative child unintentional injury incidence during 4 months, a subjective outcome with caregivers unblinded to group allocation. Secondary outcomes were caregiver knowledge, safety attitudes, and supervisory behaviors, with scores ranging from 0 to 40, 0 to 8, and 0 to 80, respectively, with higher scores indicating better knowledge, more positive safety attitudes, and more appropriate supervisory behaviors, respectively, and household environmental hazards, with scores ranging from 0 to 230 and higher scores indicating more household environmental hazards and a less safe home environment. Generalized estimating equations accounted for clustering.

Results: Among 24 randomized clusters, caregivers (mean [SD] age, 45.4 [13.0] years; 271 [75.3%] female) and children (mean [SD] age, 8.6 [2.3] years, 198 [55.0%] female) from 360 households were enrolled, with 180 each randomized to intervention and control groups. After baseline, 9 households withdrew with missing outcome data; all 360 households were included in the intention-to-treat analyses with multiple imputation. Injury occurred in 21 of 178 households (11.8%) with observed outcomes in the intervention group and 33 of 173 (19.1%) in the control group. The intervention was associated with lower injury odds (adjusted odds ratio, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.18-0.73]; P = .005). At month 4, adjusted mean differences favored the intervention for supervisory behaviors (17.08 [95% CI, 14.71-19.46] points) and household environmental hazards (-36.66 [95% CI, -42.87 to -30.46] points).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cluster randomized clinical trial of households with children aged 3 to 12 years, a civil society organization-led home visit intervention reduced caregiver-reported unintentional injuries and improved caregiver supervisory behaviors and household safety during the 4-month intervention period. Longer follow-up is needed to assess durability of the response.

item.title: Avoidable Mortality in Adults With Down Syndrome or With Other Intellectual Disabilities
item.description:
Importance: Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of Alzheimer disease. Adults with Down syndrome experience higher mortality than the general population. However, the avoidable causes and their associated factors remain unclear.

Objective: To compare the proportion and causes of avoidable mortality in adults with Down syndrome, adults with other intellectual disabilities, and the general population, and to identify factors associated with avoidable death.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based retrospective cohort study used data from the Learning From Lives and Deaths mortality review and the Office for National Statistics in England from 2016 to 2023. It included adults with Down syndrome (n = 3381), other adults with intellectual disabilities (n = 15 347), and the general population (n = 4 163 160).

Exposures: Down syndrome status, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, co-occurring health conditions, COVID-19 pandemic period.

Main outcomes and measures: Proportion and causes of avoidable, treatable, and preventable deaths according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development/Eurostat criteria; odds of avoidable death estimated using logistic regression; and age at avoidable death using Cox regression. Factors associated with avoidable death and age at death were also evaluated.

Results: Among 3381 adults with Down syndrome (1892 male [56.0%]; median [IQR] age at death, 59.5 [54.3-64.2] years), 1589 (47.0%) died from avoidable causes. Among 15 347 adults with other intellectual disabilities (8675 male [56.5%]; median [IQR] age at death, 63.8 [51.7-73.4] years), 6885 (44.9%) died from avoidable causes. Both proportions were substantially higher than in the general population (22.0%) (both P < .001). Treatable deaths were more common (972 [28.7%] vs 3847 [25.1%] vs 317 968 [7.6%]), with epilepsy and pneumonia as the leading treatable causes. Down syndrome was independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death (aOR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.25) and earlier age at avoidable death (aHR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.40-1.58). Minoritized ethnic background, asthma, diabetes, and osteoporosis were each independently associated with higher odds of avoidable death, and minoritized ethnic background and greater socioeconomic deprivation with earlier age at avoidable death.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with Down syndrome and other adults with intellectual disabilities in England, avoidable mortality exceeded that of the general population. For the adults with Down syndrome, epilepsy and pneumonia were the dominant treatable causes. These findings support proactive integrated neurological care, including epilepsy review with dementia monitoring, pneumonia prevention, and respiratory vaccination, alongside targeted interventions for minoritized ethnic groups and socioeconomically deprived groups.

item.title: Importance of Angina Pectoris by Coronary Artery Disease Severity
item.description:
Importance: Angina pectoris remains a common clinical manifestation, but contemporary population-based data on its long-term prognostic significance are limited.

Objective: To evaluate the long-term importance of angina pectoris in association with coronary artery disease (CAD) severity determined by coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) in a general population.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study included participants from the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study who had completed the Rose Questionnaire and underwent valid CCTA from November 2013 to October 2018, excluding participants with prior myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure, or coronary revascularization. Follow-up continued through September 2024. Data analyses were conducted between August 2025 and January 2026.

Exposures: Angina (defined by the Rose Questionnaire) and CAD (categorized as no findings, nonobstructive CAD [<50% stenosis], or obstructive CAD [≥50% stenosis]) according to CCTA findings.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was MI or coronary death. The secondary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as MI, coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, or death from coronary disease or heart failure. Associations were evaluated using Cox regression with sequential multivariable adjustment and stratification by CAD category and presented as hazard ratios (HRs).

Results: This study included 24 176 individuals (median [IQR] age, 57 [54-61] years; 12 225 female [50.6%]; 1615 with hyperlipidemia [6.8%]; 4374 with hypertension [18.3%]; 703 with diabetes [2.9%]). Angina was present in 720 participants (3.0%). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 7.7 (6.9-8.6) years, 293 primary events occurred. Angina was associated with a higher incidence of MI or coronary death compared with no angina (21 participants [2.9%] vs 272 participants [1.2%]; HR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.60-3.90). Event rates increased across CAD categories, with no evidence of interaction between angina and CAD severity. After multivariable adjustment, angina remained independently associated with the primary outcome (HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.04-2.63). Similar associations were observed for MACE (adjusted HR, 2.34; 95% CI, 1.73-3.16).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of a contemporary general population, angina pectoris was associated with adverse cardiac outcomes, independent of CAD severity assessed by CCTA. These findings suggest that symptom assessment remains relevant in cardiovascular risk stratification because it provided incremental prognostic information that may reflect underlying coronary microvascular dysfunction or vasomotor disorders.

item.title: Circulating Tumor DNA in Oligoprogressive Prostate Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Radiotherapy: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of a Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is increasingly used for oligoprogressive prostate cancer, but the duration of disease control is highly variable.

Objective: To evaluate time to progression based on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) prior to SBRT.

Design, setting, and participants: Between October 17, 2018, and February 1, 2023, the phase 2 prospective, single-arm, nonrandomized clinical TRAP (Targeted Radiotherapy in Androgen-Suppressed Prostate Cancer Patients) trial evaluated SBRT to treat 81 patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and 2 or fewer metastases and imaging evidence of progression while receiving an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Plasma DNA was collected at 1 or 2 points prior to SBRT and centrally tested for ctDNA using the next-generation sequencing assay PCF_SELECT. Data were collected prospectively using electronic trial case report forms. Data were extracted November 26, 2025. The median follow-up was 24.5 (IQR, 23.7-36.3) months.

Exposures: Progressing metastases were treated with SBRT, and patients were followed up with clinical assessments, serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) tests, and imaging.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome measure was time to progression, defined as an increase in serum prostate-specific antigen level of 25% or greater from the post-SBRT nadir, radiologic or symptomatic progression, clinician decision to stop ARPI, or death from any cause. The secondary outcomes were time to next therapy or death from any cause. All end points were measured from time of final SBRT treatment.

Results: Of 77 patients with evaluable blood samples taken prior to SBRT, 19 (24.7%) were in the ctDNA-positive group. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 21.1% (95% CI, 6.6%-41.0%) for the ctDNA-positive group compared with 58.3% (95% CI, 44.5%-69.8%) for the ctDNA-negative group. The median PFS was 3.0 (95% CI, 2.7-5.9) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 7.8 (95% CI, 5.9-11.4) months for the ctDNA negative group (log rank test, P = .003 at 5% significance level). The median time to initiation of a new therapy or death was 15.3 (95% CI, 4.7-26.0) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 29.6 (95% CI, 17.8-37.6) months for the ctDNA-negative group. The median overall survival was 27.2 (95% CI, 19.2 to undefined) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 33.6 (95% CI, 28.4-38.2) months for the ctDNA-negative group.

Conclusions and relevance: These findings suggest that for patients with oligoprogression and no ctDNA, SBRT and continued ARPI could be considered a valid option for prolonging disease control.

item.title: Cord Serum Neonicotinoid-Related Biomarkers and Neurodevelopment From Early to Middle Childhood
item.description:
Importance: Despite widespread neonicotinoid insecticide use, evidence on prenatal exposure and neurodevelopment beyond early childhood remains limited.

Objective: To examine whether cord serum concentrations of the neonicotinoid-related biomarkers dinotefuran and desmethyl-acetamiprid (dm-ACE) are associated with domain-specific neurodevelopment from infancy through middle childhood.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study included individuals randomly selected from eligible Hamamatsu Birth Cohort for Mothers and Children Study participants born between December 2007 and March 2012 in Japan; assessments spanned ages 10 months to 9 years. Data were analyzed between October 2025 and September 2026.

Exposures: Cord serum dinotefuran and dm-ACE concentrations measured at birth and categorized into quartiles.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes were standardized scores for 5 Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL) domains at ages 10 to 32 months and 4 Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) indices at age 9 years. Associations were examined using linear regression and expressed as mean MSEL or WISC-IV differences in SD units at quartile 3 (Q3) and Q4 concentrations (combined Q1-Q2 was the reference).

Results: Among 200 individuals, 102 (51.0%) were male and 13 (6.5%) were born preterm; 185 (92.5%) to 195 (97.5%) were included in age-specific MSEL analyses and 178 (89.0%) in WISC-IV analyses. Dinotefuran groups included 96 individuals (48.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 47 (23.5%) in Q3, and 57 (28.5%) in Q4. dm-ACE groups included 82 (41.0%) in Q1 and Q2, 63 (31.5%) in Q3, and 55 (27.5%) in Q4. Early childhood associations across neurodevelopmental scale scores varied by age and concentration group, and there were no associations after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. At age 9 years, Q3 dinotefuran concentration was associated with lower WISC-IV Processing Speed Index scores compared with Q1 to Q2 scores (mean difference, -0.50 [95% CI, -0.81 to -0.20] SDs; q = .01), and Q4 dm-ACE concentration was associated with lower Perceptual Reasoning Index scores (mean difference, -0.47 [95% CI, -0.81 to -0.14] SDs; q = .03).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of infants and children in Japan, small differences in some neurodevelopmental scale scores in early childhood were observed in association with dinotefuran and dm-ACE cord serum concentrations, but there were no associations after FDR correction. At age 9 years, dinotefuran was associated with lower processing speed and dm-ACE with lower perceptual reasoning. Overall, these findings suggest domain- and age-specific associations rather than a uniform or sustained pattern across development; confirmation in larger cohorts is needed.

Objective: To compare refracture and all-cause mortality between patients who initiated nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) and denosumab therapy after fractures.

item.title: Estimation of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccine Effectiveness in Older US Veterans
item.description:
Importance: The mRNA-1283 vaccine, a novel mRNA vaccine targeting immunodominant spike regions, was first used during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season. Older adults remain at elevated risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes, and clinical evidence of estimated vaccine effectiveness can inform seasonal vaccination policy.

Objective: To compare the estimated effectiveness of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccines against medically attended COVID-19 illness and COVID-19-associated hospitalization among US veterans aged 65 years or older.

Design, setting, and participants: This was a retrospective matched cohort study emulating a target trial. US veterans aged 65 years or older who were enrolled in a national, integrated Veterans Health Administration (VHA) health care system and received an LP.8.1-formulated mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine between August 27, 2025, and January 31, 2026, were followed up for up to 150 days or through May 1, 2026.

Exposure: Receipt of LP.8.1 mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine.

Main outcome and measures: The primary outcome was medically attended COVID-19 illness, defined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result linked to medical care or antiviral treatment or a primary COVID-19 diagnosis. Matching was performed on home county and calendar week of vaccination, followed by inverse probability of treatment weighting. Secondary outcomes included the individual component event of hospitalization. Measures were absolute and relative differences in 150-day cumulative incidence among patients receiving mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccine, computed as the estimated relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) percentage and absolute risk difference (ARD) per 10 000 persons, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors.

Results: The cohort included 60 340 mRNA-1283 and 321 845 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (mean [SD] age, 76.8 [6.7] years; 94.2% male). item.description:

Objective: To determine if implementation of an automatic tool in the EHR is associated with improved health care maintenance table updates for patients needing repeat colonoscopy for cancer screening after adenoma detection.

Eligible participants were adults aged 50 to 75 years undergoing colonoscopy for screening, surveillance, or diagnostic indications. Exclusion criteria included patients with inflammatory bowel disease, known colorectal cancer, or hereditary cancer syndromes. Data were analyzed between January and May 2025.

Exposure: A decision support tool was implemented that allowed gastroenterologists completing colonoscopies for patients with adenoma to choose follow-up intervals that would automatically populate the health maintenance tab.

Main outcomes and measures: Rate of updates of the health maintenance table and percentage completion from gastroenterology vs primary care.

item.title: Inhaled Corticosteroids and Sickle Cell Disease Severity in Adults Without Asthma: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: People living with sickle cell disease (SCD) who have episodic cough and wheeze (ECW) without a diagnosis of asthma have high rates of pain episodes and acute chest syndrome. A previous trial, in which patients with SCD and ECW without asthma received 15 weeks of inhaled mometasone or placebo, showed that inhaled mometasone improved daily pain and reduced soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), a marker of disease severity in SCD.

Objective: To examine the biologic effects and safety of long-term daily inhaled mometasone in patients without asthma but with SCD and ECW.

Design, setting, and participants: This placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial recruited patients with SCD from December 2018 to May 2022. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled mometasone or placebo for 48 weeks. Data analyses followed the modified intention-to-treat principle and were performed between July and November 2023.

Interventions: The inhaled mometasone group received 220 μg of inhaled mometasone furoate dry powder once daily. The placebo group received a matching placebo inhaler.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was percentage change in soluble VCAM-1 levels from baseline to end of study. Secondary outcomes included laboratory results, functional outcomes, patient-reported outcomes, and health care utilization.

Results: Of the 77 patients who received the intervention and were included in the analysis, 40 were assigned to inhaled mometasone (mean [SD] age, 36.0 [11.6] years; 26 females [65%]) and 37 were assigned to placebo (mean [SD] age, 31.5 [8.6] years; 19 males [51%]). Compared with the placebo group, the inhaled mometasone group increased their soluble VCAM-1 levels by 42% (95% CI, -11% to 96%; P = .02). Point estimates for clinical outcomes favored the placebo group, although the findings were not statistically significant.

Conclusions and relevance: In this trial of adults with SCD and ECW, extended courses of inhaled mometasone were associated with worsened markers of disease severity. Inhaled mometasone should not be used long-term in patients with SCD and ECW without a definitive diagnosis of asthma.

item.title: Ibuprofen Use and Acute Kidney Injury Among Adults Admitted to the Hospital
item.description:
Importance: Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the most effective nonopioid analgesics for acute pain, they may be underused in the inpatient setting due to uncertainty regarding the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI). Whether inpatient exposure to NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, substantially increases AKI risk and how ibuprofen-associated AKI varies across patient subgroups remain unknown.

Objective: To determine whether ibuprofen use is associated with AKI in hospitalized patients and whether the finding varies across AKI risk factor subgroups.

Design, setting, and participants: A retrospective active-comparator cohort study of hospitalized patients (aged ≥18 years) without end-stage kidney disease or contraindications to NSAID treatment admitted from January 1, 2004, to June 30, 2017, in a large academic health system including 3 hospitals in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, with follow-up until 48 hours after treatment end, hospital discharge, or 14 days elapsed, whichever occurred first. Analyses were conducted from March 2023 through August 2026.

Exposures: At least 24 hours of treatment with ibuprofen or oxycodone for acute pain.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was AKI, defined by changes in serum creatinine and incident kidney replacement therapy (KRT). Balancing weights were used to adjust for baseline covariates and weighted Poisson regression used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% CIs.

Results: This study included 78 656 patients (median age, 59 [IQR, 47-69] years; 38 092 females [48%]) treated with ibuprofen (n = 6313) or oxycodone (n = 72 343). There were 4799 AKI events (79% stage 1) during 270 472 days of follow-up (17.7 events per 1000 days). After adjustment for baseline differences, patients treated with ibuprofen had a higher rate of any AKI (IRR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.09-1.38), severe AKI (IRR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.08-1.72), and KRT (IRR, 3.29; 95% CI, 1.35-8.03). IRRs were greater in postoperative (IRR, 1.70 [95% CI, 1.28-2.27] vs 1.12 [95% CI, 0.98-1.28]) and critically ill (IRR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.29-2.11] vs 1.16 [95% CI, 1.02-1.33]) patients. In patients at low risk (those non-critically ill, nonpostoperative, aged <60 years without kidney dysfunction; ibuprofen, n = 2966; oxycodone, n = 20 440), ibuprofen was not associated with higher AKI risk (IRR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.75-1.18).

Conclusions and relevance: This study in an inpatient cohort found that ibuprofen was associated with higher rates of AKI and KRT, but this excess risk was concentrated in patients at high risk. Patients at low risk may be able to receive ibuprofen safely yet were often prescribed oxycodone.

item.title: High-Sensitivity Troponin Pathway and Emergency Department Length of Stay
item.description:
Importance: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the diagnostic standard for acute coronary syndrome but present significant implementation and workflow complexity.

Objective: To evaluate whether implementation of a structured, electronic health record (EHR)-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with changes in emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS) and serial troponin testing times.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective quality improvement study compared preimplementation conventional cTn assay (June 1, 2021, to March 31, 2022) with a postimplementation integrated hs-cTn pathway (June 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023) in 4 urban EDs within a single health system. Participants were adults (aged ≥18 years) presenting with chest pain and at least 1 troponin assay result. Data analysis was performed from April to September 2024.

Exposures: Implementation of an hs-cTn assay within an EHR-integrated clinical pathway.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was ED LOS, defined as time from patient registration to ED departure. Secondary outcomes included time from first clinician evaluation to disposition (discharge or admission) and interval from the first troponin assay order to the second troponin assay result in patients with serial assays.

Results: Of the 16 094 patient encounters analyzed (9151 [56.9%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.5 [17.4] years), 8486 (52.7%) were in the hs-cTn and 7608 (47.3%) were in the conventional cTn cohort. Overall, hs-cTn implementation with workflow integration was associated with decreased mean ED LOS, from 6.18 (95% CI, 6.10-6.26) hours to 5.64 (95% CI, 5.57-5.71) hours. Compared with conventional cTn, implementation of the hs-cTn pathway was associated with shorter mean ED LOS in admitted patients (9.60 [95% CI, 9.35-9.87] hours vs 10.50 [95% CI, 10.22-10.78] hours; P = .003) and discharged patients (5.02 [95% CI, 4.96-5.08] hours vs 5.33 [95% CI, 5.26-5.40] hours; P = .006). Pathway implementation was also associated with shorter time from evaluation to disposition in patients receiving 2 or more troponin measurements (5.06 [95% CI, 4.97-5.15] hours vs 6.68 [95% CI, 6.52-6.85] hours; P < .001) and time from first troponin order to second troponin result in both admitted patients (3.18 [95% CI, 3.11-3.25] hours vs 5.16 [95% CI, 5.01-5.31] hours; P < .001) and discharged patients (2.78 [95% CI, 2.75-2.82] hours vs 4.54 [95% CI, 4.46-4.62] hours; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, an EHR-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with significantly reduced ED LOS and, in patients with serial troponin measurements, reduced time from evaluation to disposition and reduced time to serial assay results. The findings suggest this structured EHR approach may mitigate operational challenges of hs-cTn adoption and could serve as a scalable model to improve ED efficiency for patients with chest pain.

item.title: Opioid Use and Overdose in Patients With Solid Tumor Cancers
item.description:
Importance: Opioids are essential for symptom control, but few studies have evaluated the association between prescription opioids and opioid overdose in oncology.

Objective: To describe opioid overdose in adults with solid tumor cancers and examine how opioid overdose rates vary by patient factors, cancer characteristics, and opioid prescribing.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based, retrospective cohort study of adults in Ontario, Canada, used linked ICES data from January 1, 2013, to December 31, 2020. Participants entered the cohort at the time of newly diagnosed solid tumor cancers and were followed up from diagnosis to the first opioid overdose event, death, or December 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from August to December 2025.

Exposure: Exposure was outpatient opioid prescription dose and duration reassessed every 30 days.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was a fatal or the first nonfatal opioid overdose event.

Results: Among 554 316 adults with cancer (mean [SD] age, 63.8 [16.2], 57.1 [17.2], and 45.8 [13.7] years for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively; 308 903 [55.9%], 921 [59.5%], and 116 [60.7%] female for the no, nonfatal, and fatal opioid overdose groups, respectively), 1591 (0.3%) had 1 or more nonfatal opioid overdoses, and 191 (0.03%) had a fatal opioid overdose. In the first year after diagnosis, patients with stage III and IV cancers had substantially higher rates of any opioid overdose than those with stage I (stage III vs I: hazard ratio [HR], 2.55; 95% CI, 1.96-3.31; stage IV vs I: HR, 6.24; 95% CI, 4.68-8.31). After adjustment, any opioid prescription in the prior 30 days was associated with 71% higher combined nonfatal and fatal opioid overdose rate (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.47-2.00), and approximately 3.5 times higher if prescribed high-dose opioids (≥50-mg morphine-equivalent daily dose; HR, 3.47; 95% CI, 2.97-4.05). Recently prescribed opioids were associated with increased opioid overdose risk in patients with cancer without opioid use disorder (any dose: HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.54-2.11; high dose: HR, 3.76; 95% CI, 3.21-4.41).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with solid tumor cancers, opioid overdose was rare and highest in the first year after diagnosis and in patients with advanced cancer; opioid overdose risk increased with every month high-dose opioids were prescribed. The findings suggest that opioids should be prescribed at the lowest effective dose for symptom management, with close monitoring and routine assessment for opioid overdose risk.

item.title: Chemotherapy-Induced Biological Age Acceleration and Lifetime Outcomes in Breast Cancer Survivors
item.description:
Importance: Growing evidence suggests some breast cancer survivors may experience accelerated aging (biological age in excess of chronological age) after receiving chemotherapy.

Objective: To quantify the range of lifetime changes in accelerated aging following chemotherapy.

Design, setting, and participants: This comparative effectiveness study used an established Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network breast cancer model integrating biological aging with breast cancer epidemiology. Biological aging was modeled using data on distributions of postchemotherapy senescence measured by p16INK4a levels, and the model assumed chemotherapy-induced senescence only affected non-breast cancer mortality. The simulated population included US women diagnosed with breast cancer at ages 30 to 79 years between 1990 and 2030, with follow-up until death. Two model simulations were run; the first assumed all women who developed breast cancer received anthracycline, and the second assumed all received nonanthracycline treatment. Modeling was conducted from November 2025 to April 2026. Results were validated by comparing model-predicted trends with findings from the Anthracycline for Early Breast Cancer (ABC) trials.

Exposures: More vs less cytotoxic chemotherapy, using exemplar anthracycline-based vs nonanthracycline regimens.

Main outcomes and measures: Lifetime outcomes included the age at which the risk of non-breast cancer mortality exceeded the risk of breast cancer mortality by chemotherapy regimen, posttreatment life-years, and all-cause mortality by age group at diagnosis and median senescence levels.

Results: The study included a simulated population of 400 million US women aged 30 to 79 years diagnosed with breast cancer. Breast cancer survivors who received anthracycline lost 9.4 (IQR, 7.6-11.2) years of remaining life years. Overall, among anthracycline recipients, the risk of non-breast cancer mortality was projected to exceed breast cancer mortality 16 (IQR, 12-19) years earlier than expected based on chronological age. There was heterogeneity in results, with greater variability for women diagnosed at younger vs older ages. Women receiving more vs less cytotoxic regimens were estimated to lose a median difference of 7.6 (IQR, 7.0-8.0) more years of life due to earlier ages at onset of aging-related diseases. The model closely replicated all-cause and 8-year breast cancer survival trends in the ABC trials.

Conclusions and relevance: In this simulation model of chemotherapy-induced biological aging, increased breast cancer survival was seen with more (vs less) cytotoxic regimens, but this was paired with greater potential risk of earlier non-breast cancer mortality due to age acceleration. These results suggest the value of integrating knowledge about biological aging into survivorship care and could inform future research to address accelerated aging among breast cancer survivors.

item.title: Differences in Health and Access to Care Between Heterosexual and Sexual Minority Health Care Professionals
item.description:
Importance: Little is known about the health and access to care of sexual minority health care professionals (HCPs).

Objective: To compare health outcomes, health insurance coverage, and access to care between sexual minority and heterosexual HCPs.

Design, setting, and participants: For this survey study, cross-sectional data analysis of the 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024 National Health Interview Surveys was performed. The study population included nationally representative household probability samples of noninstitutionalized US civilian adults aged 18 years or older, restricted to HCPs working in health care settings. Data analysis was conducted between February 2024 and August 2026.

Exposure: Self-reported sexual orientation, categorized as sexual minority (gay, lesbian, bisexual, or another nonheterosexual identity) or heterosexual.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes included cigarette smoking, lifetime diagnosis of depression, moderate to severe psychological distress, selected physical health conditions, primary source of health insurance coverage, and delayed or forgone medical care, mental health care, and prescription medications due to cost. Multivariable logistic regression models compared outcomes while adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics.

Results: The sample included 2890 HCPs (2731 heterosexual and 159 sexual minority; mean [SE] age, 44.9 [0.7] years; 74.7% [0.9%] female [survey weighted]). Sexual minority individuals represented 5.7% (95% CI, 4.8%-6.7%) of HCPs and were more likely to be younger (aged 26-34 years: 38.8% [95% CI, 30.1%-48.3%] vs 24.0% [95% CI, 22.2%-25.9%]), never married (32.7% [95% CI, 24.7%-41.8%] vs 14.6% [95% CI, 13.0%-16.4%]), and living in households below the federal poverty level (7.4% [95% CI, 3.4%-15.4%] vs 1.1% [95% CI, 0.7%-1.7%]) compared with heterosexual HCPs. Sexual minority HCPs were significantly more likely to report a lifetime diagnosis of depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.05 [95% CI, 2.02-4.59]), moderate to severe psychological distress (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.23-3.46]), arthritis (AOR, 2.45 [95% CI, 1.42-4.22]), and delayed medical care due to cost (AOR, 2.06 [95% CI, 1.14-3.72]). Sexual minority HCPs faced greater disparities in access to care: they were more likely to forgo mental health care (AOR, 3.74 [95% CI, 2.11-6.63]) and to forgo prescription medications (AOR, 4.81 [95% CI, 2.52-9.15]) due to cost than their heterosexual peers.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional survey study of HCPs, sexual minority HCPs were more likely than heterosexual HCPs to report depression, psychological distress, and financial barriers to health care. These findings highlight disparities in health and access to care among sexual minority HCPs and the need for workplace supports to address factors contributing to these disparities.

item.title: Social Determinants of Health and Long-Term, Device-Based Sleep Health
item.description:
Importance: Prior research on social determinants of health (SDOH) and sleep health has largely relied on subjective sleep measures, primarily self-reported sleep duration. Evidence remains limited on the associations between SDOH and wearable-derived long-term sleep patterns in large-scale populations.

Objective: To examine how SDOH (overall and by domain) are associated with long-term, wearable-derived sleep duration and variability.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study included participants from the All of Us Research Program enrolled between 2018 and 2023 who contributed at least 180 days of wearable data, including pre-enrollment historical records, and completed the SDOH survey. Data analysis was conducted from September 2025 to June 2026.

Exposures: Measures of overall and domain-specific SDOH, including social and community context, economic stability, neighborhood environment, and health care access and quality, were derived from validated surveys and standardized to z scores.

Main outcomes and measures: Mean daily sleep duration (in minutes) and day-to-day sleep duration SD across all available days were calculated from device-estimated main sleep episodes.

Results: Among 12 403 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.8 [15.2] years; 8719 female [70.3%]; 10 946 White [88.3%] and 1457 members of minority racial groups [11.7%]; 756 Hispanic [6.1%]), 9052 individuals (73.0%) had a college degree or above, with a mean (SD) sleep duration of 406.1 (44.9) minutes and a mean (SD) sleep duration SD of 76.9 (20.6) minutes. Participants were monitored for a median (range) of 982 (180 to 4133) days. Compared with participants in the lowest SDOH tertile, those in the highest tertile (indicating more favorable social and structural conditions) had 5.82 minutes (95% CI, 3.84 to 7.80 minutes) longer sleep duration and 4.79 minutes (95% CI, -5.69 to -3.89 minutes) lower sleep duration SD in the fully adjusted model. When examining individual SDOH domains, economic stability showed the strongest associations with mean sleep duration (eg, 10.70 minutes; 95% CI, 5.30 to 16.10 minutes) and sleep duration SD (eg, -8.70 minutes; 95% CI, -11.20 to -6.26 minutes). Limited subgroup heterogeneity in the association was observed across age, sex, race, and ethnicity.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, more favorable SDOH conditions were associated with longer and more regular habitual sleep duration over the long term, emphasizing the importance of social and structural factors when evaluating sleep health.

item.title: Inforatio Technique and Foot Ulcer Closure Among Patients With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are common complications of diabetes, a disease increasing in prevalence worldwide. Novel adjunctive treatments that are affordable and feasible to implement in both high- and low-income settings are urgently needed.

Objective: To assess whether the inforatio technique promotes healing of DFUs compared with standard of care (SOC).

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, evaluator-blinded randomized clinical trial was conducted at 4 outpatient clinics specializing in wound care in Denmark from February 15, 2022, to December 18, 2024. One-year medical record follow-up was completed August 14, 2025. Participants included patients with noninfected Wagner grade 1 DFUs.

Interventions: Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive the inforatio technique every third week for 12 weeks with SOC or SOC only. The inforatio technique involved making incisions on wound beds with 2-mm biopsy punch tools.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of ulcers achieving closure within 20 weeks. Secondary outcomes were health-related and disease-specific quality of life. Safety outcomes included serious and target ulcer-related adverse events.

Results: A total of 101 patients were randomized, of whom 100 had DFUs and were included in the primary analysis (49 in the inforatio group and 51 in the SOC only group; 85 men; mean [SD] age, 64.4 [11.4] years; median ulcer size, 0.76 [range, 0.09-23.23] cm2). Twenty-four patients in the inforatio group (49.0%) vs 14 in the SOC-only group (27.5%) achieved ulcer closure within 20 weeks (adjusted odds ratio, 3.01 [95% CI, 1.20-7.58]; P = .02). No between-group difference was found in quality of life change from baseline to 20 weeks. Within 20 weeks, 7 patients in the inforatio group vs 13 in the SOC-only group experienced the serious adverse events, including death, amputation, or target ulcer-related hospitalization (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.24-1.29]; P = .25), and 16 patients in the inforatio group vs 30 in the SOC-only group experienced target ulcer-related adverse events (relative risk, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.88]; P = .02).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, the inforatio technique improved DFU healing compared with SOC alone. Fewer ulcer-related adverse events were also observed with the inforatio technique, although this exploratory finding should be interpreted cautiously.
