item.title: Neighborhood Social Disadvantage and Lung Aging and Mortality
item.description:
Importance: Neighborhood social disadvantage (NSD) is increasingly recognized as being associated with health disparities. However, its associations with longitudinal lung function decline, health-related quality of life (HRQOL), and mortality remain incompletely understood.

Objective: To evaluate associations of NSD with lung function, HRQOL, and all-cause mortality and to explore potential mediators of any association.

Design, setting, and participants: Prospective cohort study of current and former smokers aged 40 to 75 years with at least 10 pack-years of smoking history in the Lovelace Smokers Cohort. Participants underwent repeated spirometry approximately every 18 months from 2001 through 2017. Mortality was ascertained through October 2020 using the National Death Index. Data were analyzed from January to May 2025.

Exposures: Census tract-level Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Social Deprivation Index (SDI) assigned to residential addresses.

Main outcomes and measures: Baseline and longitudinal lung function (forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1], forced vital capacity [FVC], and the FEV1:FVC ratio), baseline HRQOL assessed by the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), with higher scores indicating poorer respiratory health status, and the 36-item Short Form Survey, and all-cause mortality. Formal mediation analyses evaluated educational attainment, current smoking status, and dietary patterns, whereas baseline lung function and HRQOL were considered as potential mediators for associations of NSD with all-cause mortality.

Results: Among 2362 included participants, the mean (SD) baseline age was 56.3 (9.4) years, and 1738 (73.58%) were female. A 1-IQR increase in SDI was associated with lower baseline FEV1 (β, -0.09 [95% CI, -0.13 to -0.06] L) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, -1.21 [95% CI, -1.80 to -0.62] percentage points). Higher SVI was associated with faster annual decline in FEV1 (β, -3.11 [95% CI, -5.86 to -0.36] mL/y) and FEV1:FVC ratio (β, -0.05 [95% CI, -0.11 to -0.001] percentage points/y), worse baseline HRQOL, including a higher SGRQ total score (β, 4.46 [95% CI, 3.26-5.65] points), and higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.08-1.53]). Current smoking status and 2 dietary pattern scores mediated 4.4% (95% CI, -1.2% to 12.8%) to 31.0% (95% CI, 13.0%-51.6%) and 4.5% (95% CI, 0.2%-12.9%) to 17.0% (95% CI, 5.5%-113.7%), respectively, of selected associations between NSD and lung health outcomes; baseline lung function and HRQOL mediated 6.7% (95% CI, 0.6%-22.8%) to 38.6% (95% CI, 19.9%-125.3%) of selected associations with all-cause mortality.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, worse NSD was associated with faster lung function decline, worse HRQOL, and higher all-cause mortality among ever smokers. Mediation analyses suggested that current smoking status and dietary patterns may partially account for associations of NSD with lung function and HRQOL.

item.title: Perioperative Antibiotic Use in Head and Neck Surgery
item.description:
Importance: Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis in head and neck surgery remains poorly standardized internationally, despite evidence supporting short-course regimens and showing no benefit in low-risk procedures. Contemporary international data on prescribing practice are limited.

Objectives: To characterize international patterns of perioperative antibiotic use in endocrine and oncologic head and neck surgery and to identify discrepancies between reported practice and evidence-based recommendations.

Design, setting, and participants: In this survey study, a cross-sectional survey was distributed electronically between October 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025, through national and international professional societies. Respondents were classified by country of practice into Europe, North America, and rest of world. Data were analyzed in June 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Routine antibiotic use, agent selection, and duration of prophylaxis across 6 procedure categories (conventional thyroidectomy, completion thyroidectomy, complex thyroidectomy, low-risk head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [HNSCC], low-complexity HNSCC, and complex clean-contaminated HNSCC). Secondary outcomes were departmental guideline availability and circumstances prompting antibiotic use.

Results: Of 468 respondents (310 of 419 [74%] with available data reported male sex or gender, 32 of 432 [82%] otolaryngologists-head and neck surgeons and 283 of 431 [66%] in academic practice), routine antibiotic use for conventional thyroidectomy was reported by 12% (95% CI, 8%-19%) of European, 35% (95% CI, 27%-44%) of North American, and 56% (95% CI, 39%-71%) of rest of world respondents. For clean-contaminated HNSCC, prophylaxis use ranged from 93% to 99%, with aminopenicillin plus a β-lactamase inhibitor preferred in Europe (66%) and North America (64%); cefazolin predominated in North America (47%) and cefuroxime in Europe (31%). For low-complexity clean-contaminated procedures, 24-hour regimens were reported by 43% (95% CI, 34%-53%) of North American vs 11% (95% CI, 7%-16%) of European respondents, whereas 7-day courses were reported by 23% (95% CI, 17%-29%) of European vs 8% (95% CI, 4%-15%) of North American respondents. Departmental HNSCC guidelines were more available in Europe than North America (83% vs 38%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this survey study of 468 head and neck surgeons, perioperative antibiotic prescribing was heterogeneous internationally, with routine use in clean procedures and prolonged regimens for clean-contaminated surgery. Departmental guideline availability did not correspond to shorter reported prophylaxis duration, suggesting that implementation rather than guideline existence may be the target for antimicrobial stewardship.
